India–US Relations Since 1947

India–US relations have evolved from Cold War-era differences and strategic distance into a broad-based strategic partnership covering defence, technology, trade, energy, space, critical minerals and the Indo-Pacific.

The Beginning: 1947–1962

India and the United States established diplomatic relations in 1946, even before India became independent.

After independence, India followed a policy of Non-Alignment, choosing not to formally join either the US-led or Soviet-led Cold War blocs.

The two countries nevertheless cooperated in:

• Economic and development assistance
• Food security and agriculture
• Education and scientific cooperation
• Economic and technical assistance

However, the United States developed close security ties with Pakistan, while India maintained increasingly close relations with the Soviet Union.

1962: India-China War
The 1962 India-China War created temporary strategic convergence.

The United States provided military assistance to India during the conflict, demonstrating that shared concerns over China could create space for cooperation.

The Difficult Phase: 1960s–1980s

Relations remained complicated because of Cold War geopolitics.

1971: India–Pakistan War

The 1971 India–Pakistan War became one of the lowest points in India–US relations. US supported Pakistan, while India had signed the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation.

The episode reinforced India's perception of the US as being strategically aligned with Pakistan.

1974: India's First Nuclear Test

India conducted its first nuclear test at Pokhran in 1974. US strongly opposed India's nuclear programme, and nuclear proliferation became a major source of tension.

Overall Character of the Cold War Period

India–US relations were shaped by:

• India's Non-Alignment
• US–Pakistan relations
• India–Soviet relations
• Nuclear differences
• Different approaches to Cold War politics

The relationship was therefore marked by strategic distance despite shared democratic values.

The Turning Point: 1991–2000

The end of the Cold War fundamentally changed the relationship. India also introduced economic liberalisation in 1991, creating new opportunities for trade, investment and technology cooperation. The collapse of the Soviet Union reduced the geopolitical importance of the earlier India–US divide.

1998: Nuclear Tests
India conducted nuclear tests at Pokhran in May 1998. The United States imposed sanctions, but diplomatic engagement continued.

1999: Kargil War

The Kargil War became an important turning point. The United States pressured Pakistan to withdraw its forces from the Line of Control.This contributed to greater strategic understanding between India and the US.

2000: Clinton's Visit

US President Bill Clinton's visit to India in 2000 marked a major improvement in bilateral relations.The relationship increasingly shifted from Cold War differences towards economic and strategic engagement.

Strategic Partnership: 2000–2008

The early 21st century witnessed a major transformation.

2005: Civil Nuclear Deal

The India–US Civil Nuclear Agreement became a landmark breakthrough.

It enabled greater civilian nuclear cooperation with India despite India not being a member of the NPT. The agreement eventually contributed to the 2008 NSG waiver, allowing India to participate in international civilian nuclear commerce.

Why It Was Important

• Reduced India's nuclear isolation.
• Opened civilian nuclear cooperation.
• Increased strategic trust.
• Recognised India's growing global importance.
• Fundamentally changed the bilateral relationship.

Defence Partnership: 2010s

Defence cooperation expanded rapidly.

The two countries increased:

• Military exercises
• Defence trade
• Maritime security cooperation
• Intelligence sharing
• Defence technology cooperation

India was designated a Major Defense Partner by the United States in 2016.

Major Defence Agreements

• LEMOA – 2016 Logistics support and access between the armed forces.

• COMCASA – 2018 Secure communications and interoperability.

• BECA – 2020 Sharing of geospatial information and advanced military data.

These agreements strengthened military cooperation while supporting India's defence modernisation.

Indo-Pacific: A New Strategic Pillar

The rise of China and growing strategic competition in the Indo-Pacific have created greater convergence between India and the United States.

The two countries cooperate through the Quad, along with Japan and Australia.

Areas of cooperation include:

• Maritime security
• Freedom of navigation
• Supply-chain resilience
• Critical technologies
• Humanitarian assistance and disaster relief
• A free, open and inclusive Indo-Pacific
The Indo-Pacific has therefore become one of the central pillars of contemporary India–US relations.

Technology & Emerging Sectors
The relationship has expanded beyond traditional defence and diplomacy.

Critical & Emerging Technology cooperation includes:

• Artificial Intelligence
• Semiconductors
• Quantum technology
• Biotechnology
• Telecommunications
• Cybersecurity

The Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET) has strengthened cooperation in these areas.

Space

India and the US cooperate in:

• Earth observation
• Satellite technology
• Space exploration
• Human spaceflight
• Space situational awareness

Critical Minerals

Both countries are working towards resilient supply chains for minerals essential for:

• Electric vehicles
• Batteries
• Renewable energy
• Semiconductors
• Defence technology

Economic Relationship

The United States is one of India's most important economic partners.
Major areas include:
• Trade and investment
• Information technology
• Pharmaceuticals
• Electronics
• Defence manufacturing
• Energy
• Digital economy
• Services

The Indian diaspora in the United States also acts as an important bridge between the two countries.
Current Situation: 2025–26

The return of Donald Trump to the US presidency in January 2025 has introduced a more transactional dimension to the relationship.

Strategic cooperation remains strong, but trade, tariffs and India's relationship with Russia have emerged as major areas of friction.

Strategic Cooperation Continues

Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump met in February 2025 and reaffirmed the importance of the bilateral relationship.

The two sides focused on:

• Defence cooperation
• Trade and investment
• Critical and emerging technologies
• Critical minerals
• Energy security
• Space cooperation
• Indo-Pacific security

Thus, despite disagreements, the strategic foundation of the relationship remains strong.

Trade & Tariffs :
Trade has become one of the major areas of tension.
The Trump administration has pushed for:
• Lower Indian tariffs
• Greater market access for US goods
• Reduction of trade barriers
• A more balanced trade relationship

India and the US have continued negotiations towards a broader bilateral trade agreement.

The key challenge is balancing:

US demand for greater market access with India's protection of domestic producers and strategic sectors.

Russia: A Major Test

India's continued defence and energy relationship with Russia remains a sensitive issue. The United States has sought to pressure countries to reduce dependence on Russian energy.
India, however, continues to emphasise:
• Energy security
• Strategic autonomy
• National interest
• Independent foreign-policy decision-making
This creates a difficult balancing act for India.

India wants stronger ties with US without compromising its long-standing relationship with Russia.

Defence: Strongest Area of Convergence

Defence remains one of the strongest pillars of India–US relations.
Cooperation includes:
• Defence procurement
• Military exercises
• Maritime security
• Intelligence and surveillance
• Defence technology
• Co-production
• Indo-Pacific security

The relationship is increasingly moving from buyer–seller relations towards technology sharing and defence co-production.

China & the Indo-Pacific

China remains an important factor behind India–US strategic convergence.

Both countries seek:

• A free and open Indo-Pacific
• Secure sea lanes
• Resilient supply chains
• Greater maritime cooperation
• Reduced dependence on vulnerable supply chains

However, India does not want its relationship with the United States to become a formal anti-China alliance.

India's approach remains:
Strategic cooperation + Strategic autonomy

Why India–US Relations Are Strategically Important ?

1. Indo-Pacific Security
The US is an important partner in India's effort to maintain a free, open, inclusive and rules-based Indo-Pacific.

2. Defence Modernisation
US defence technology and cooperation can strengthen India's military capabilities and domestic defence manufacturing.

3. China

Growing Chinese influence has created greater strategic convergence between India and the US.

4. Technology

Cooperation in AI, semiconductors, quantum technology and space can strengthen India's technological capabilities.

5. Economic Security

Both countries have an interest in diversified and resilient supply chains.

6. Global Governance

India and the US increasingly cooperate on global challenges while India seeks a greater role in institutions such as the UN Security Council and other multilateral platforms.

India's Approach: Partnership Without Alliance

India's relationship with the US reflects its broader foreign-policy principle of strategic autonomy.
India cooperates closely with US on:
• Defence
• Technology
• Indo-Pacific security
• Counter-terrorism
• Critical minerals

At the same time, India maintains important relations with:
• Russia
• European countries
• Japan
• ASEAN
• West Asian countries

This reflects India's approach of multi-alignment — cooperating with different powers according to national interests rather than becoming part of a fixed alliance bloc.

India–US relations have travelled a long distance since 1947 from Cold War-era strategic distance to a comprehensive strategic partnership.The relationship today covers defence, technology, trade, space, critical minerals, energy and Indo-Pacific security. At the same time, differences over tariffs, trade, Russia and energy policy demonstrate that the partnership is not an alliance.

For India, the objective is to cooperate with the United States where interests converge, manage differences where they exist, and preserve strategic autonomy.

ACCOUNTABILITY UNDER PRESSURE: IS CRITICISM BEING TREATED AS A THREAT?

Journalist Sohit Mishra raises a fundamental democratic question: what happens to accountability when those in power become increasingly insulated from scrutiny?

The argument presented in the video is not merely about one blocked post, one raid or one media organisation. It is about a broader pattern in which criticism of the government can encounter institutional, financial, regulatory or digital pressure.

According to the video, an Indian Express report stated that the Government of India issued orders between March and July 2026 resulting in around 1.95 lakh pieces of online content being blocked. If that figure and timeframe are accurately reported, the scale is extraordinary—roughly 1,275 pieces of content a day. But the underlying categories, legal grounds and individual blocking orders matter enormously; a numerical total alone cannot establish whether every blocking action was politically motivated.

The larger issue is therefore transparency.

A democratic government has the legal authority to restrict unlawful content in appropriate circumstances. But democracy also requires that citizens should be able to know:

• What was blocked?
• Under which law?
• On whose complaint or recommendation?
• For what specific reason?
• Was the affected publisher notified?
• Was there an effective appeal mechanism?
• How many orders were challenged successfully?

Without such transparency, a legitimate power to regulate unlawful content can gradually become an instrument capable of suppressing legitimate criticism.

THE MEDIA QUESTION

The video places the contemporary digital environment in a longer political history.

It recalls the BBC documentary controversy concerning the 2002 Gujarat riots and then points to subsequent developments involving major media organisations and journalists.

For example, Income Tax authorities conducted searches at the premises of Raghav Bahl, founder of The Quint, and The Quint's offices in October 2018. The authorities described the action as part of an investigation into alleged tax-related irregularities.

In 2019, the Enforcement Directorate registered a money-laundering case against Bahl based on Income Tax Department material concerning alleged undisclosed foreign assets. Bahl denied wrongdoing and maintained that the relevant investments had been disclosed.

These facts require an important distinction:

An investigation or raid is not, by itself, proof of political persecution.

But equally, the existence of a legal justification does not automatically eliminate the possibility of intimidation or chilling effects.

That is precisely why independent institutions, judicial oversight, transparent procedures and a genuinely plural media ecosystem matter.

THE REAL TEST IS ACCOUNTABILITY

The strongest democratic test is not whether a government can silence unlawful speech.

Every constitutional democracy needs mechanisms against incitement, terrorism, fraud, harassment and other genuinely unlawful conduct.

The real test is whether the government can tolerate lawful, uncomfortable and persistent criticism.

A government confident in its record should welcome scrutiny.

A government accountable to citizens should answer difficult questions.

A government committed to constitutional democracy should not confuse criticism of the government with hostility towards the nation.

And citizens should never be asked to choose between national interest and freedom of expression. In a constitutional democracy, protecting legitimate freedom of expression is itself a national interest.

THE QUESTION INDIA SHOULD ASK

The debate therefore should not be reduced to:

“Is the government allowed to block content?”

The more important questions are:

How much content is being blocked?

Why is it being blocked?

Who decides?

How transparent is the process?

How often are those decisions independently reviewed?

hitting our $1.2M ARR wasn't about going viral or huge ad spend.

it was boring, tiny site tweaks most people miss.

here are the 8 steps & prompts that boosted your traffic and conversions:

0. Understand the Full System

website optimization isn’t just about changing the design.

it comes down to three stages:

① build a foundation Google and AI can crawl and understand
② attract visitors with useful content
③ use data to turn those visitors into signups and purchases

ranking on Google isn’t enough.

if AI engines can’t understand your content—or visitors land on your site but don’t understand the value—you still won’t get results.

the key is identifying which stage is broken and improving it with a clear goal.

if you want to improve your website or grow your organic traffic, bookmark this.

1. Understand What’s Happening With Data

the first step is making sure you can see what is actually happening.

not guesses. real data.

the two main tools you need are Google Analytics 4 (GA4) and Google Search Console (GSC).

both are free.

GA4 shows what people do after they visit your website:

・which pages get the most traffic
・whether visitors come from Google, social media, or other channels
・whether visitors come from AI tools like ChatGPT or Perplexity
・which pages lead to signups or purchases

Google Search Console shows how people discover you through Google:

・which keywords your pages appear for
・how many people click from search results
・your average search position
・which articles are gaining or losing rankings

with these two tools, you can separate two very different problems:

“not enough people are visiting”

vs.

“people are visiting, but they aren’t taking action”

connect GA4 and Google Search Console to NoimosAI, and it can analyze the data and suggest what to improve.

feed these prompts into NoimosAI to identify the room for improvement:
“Analyze traffic from Google Search and AI search engines using GA4 and GSC, then recommend the pages with the highest improvement potential.”

“Using GSC data, identify articles that have lost rankings and recommend which ones should be rewritten.”

2. Build a Technical Foundation Google and AI Can Understand

you can create the most useful content in your industry.

but if Google and AI can’t properly crawl and understand it, people won’t find it through search results or AI-generated answers.

here’s what to check:

・are your important pages indexed by Google?
・does your sitemap tell crawlers which pages exist?
・is robots.txt accidentally blocking Google or AI crawlers?
・does the site load quickly and work well on mobile?
・are there broken links or layout issues?
・does JSON-LD clearly identify your company, products, and articles?
・does llms.txt organize your most important pages for AI?

robots.txt, sitemaps, and JSON-LD create a shared technical foundation for both traditional search and AI search.

the work that helps Google discover and understand your pages is called technical SEO.

GEO goes one step further by making your content easier for AI engines to understand and use in their answers.

NoimosAI can analyze page speed, site structure, robots.txt, JSON-LD, and other technical issues—then recommend improvements for both search engines and AI.

use this prompt in NoimosAI to optimize your site:
“Audit [Website URL] for search engine and AI readability. Analyze robots.txt, the sitemap, JSON-LD, llms.txt, and page speed, then recommend specific improvements.”

3. Communicate Your Value Above the Fold

visitors decide within seconds whether they want to keep reading.

the first screen they see should answer three questions:

・who is this for?
・what problem does it solve?
・what should I do next?

listing dozens of features won’t help if visitors can’t see why the product matters to them.

for example, describing NoimosAI as “a powerful AI agent” is too abstract.

“delegate your marketing work to AI” makes the outcome much easier to understand.

don’t just describe the product.

show people what changes after they use it.

prompt to find the best messages for your site:
“Analyze the first screen visitors see on [Website URL], then suggest a headline and supporting copy that communicate the value immediately.”

4. Give People a Reason to Trust You and Take Action

interest alone doesn’t create signups.

even when people understand your service, they may still wonder:

“does this actually work?”

“will this work for my company?”

your website needs to answer those questions with evidence.

use things like:

・real product screenshots
・specific use cases
・customer results
・testimonials
・supported integrations
・security information
・pricing and the steps required to get started

don’t add everything just to make the page longer.

choose the proof that addresses the biggest concerns customers have before signing up.

on the NoimosAI website, we show the product, supported services, customer testimonials, and security information before guiding visitors toward getting started.

5. Choose Keywords That Can Generate Revenue

once the foundation is ready, you need to attract the right visitors.

a better website won’t generate results if nobody sees it.

start with the problems your customers are already searching for on Google.

then create articles that solve those problems and introduce your product as one possible solution.

the key: don’t target a keyword just because it has high search volume.

for example, “best AI tools” may get a lot of searches, but it is extremely competitive.

more specific keywords like:

“best AI tools for social media posts”

or:

“best AI tools for competitor analysis”

usually have clearer intent and less competition.

use data from Semrush or similar tools to find keywords that:

・match a real problem your customers have
・have enough search volume to matter
・aren’t dominated by impossible competition
・show comparison, evaluation, or purchase intent

a good keyword doesn’t just generate traffic.

it attracts people who could eventually become customers.

use this prompt to find the best keywords to get visitors:
“Find keywords that customers of [Product or Service] are searching for. Organize them by search volume, ranking difficulty, and search intent.”

6. Create Articles That Rank on Google and Get Understood by AI

once you choose a keyword, analyze the pages already ranking for it.

top-ranking pages reveal what people are expecting to find.

but copying the same information gives people no reason to read your article.

first, analyze the SEO side:

・what topics appear across most top-ranking articles?
・what order makes the information easiest to understand?
・what information is missing?
・what information is outdated?
・where can you add your own experience or data?

then make the structure easy for AI to understand:

・answer one clear question under each heading
・give the direct answer first
・summarize the most important points
・include examples, numbers, and sources
・add an FAQ at the end

don’t write an FAQ that avoids the question.

answer it directly in the first one or two sentences, then explain the reasoning and examples.

this makes the article easier for readers to scan and easier for AI to extract useful answers from.

that’s a core part of GEO.

NoimosAI can analyze Google search results, create the article structure, write the content, and include summaries, direct answers, and FAQs designed for both SEO and GEO.

prompt:
“Analyze the top-ranking search results for [Keyword], then create an SEO/GEO-optimized article targeting that keyword.”

7. Use Data to Find What to Improve

publishing a page is not the finish line.

algorithms change. information becomes outdated. customer behavior changes.

you need to keep improving based on what the data tells you.

the same “underperforming page” can have completely different problems:

・high search impressions, but few clicks
　→ the title or description isn’t compelling enough

・high rankings, but little traffic
　→ the keyword may have low search demand

・high traffic, but few signups
　→ the content, CTA, page flow, or trust signals may be weak

・an article used to perform, but rankings dropped
　→ the information may be outdated, or competitors may now offer better content

don’t try to fix every page at once.

identify the cause, then start with the pages where a small improvement could create the biggest result.

prompt to use in NoimosAI:
“Using GSC and GA4, categorize pages into: ① pages that don’t appear in search, ② pages that appear but don’t get clicked, and ③ pages that get traffic but don’t generate signups. Recommend improvements for each.”

8. Compare Before and After, Then Keep Improving

website optimization is never a one-time project.

when you change a title, check the click-through rate.

when you update an article, check its search ranking.

when you change the page structure, check the signup rate.

record every change and compare the numbers before and after.

that’s how you learn which improvements are actually driving results.

here’s what we review every month:

・pages gaining or losing search impressions
・pages gaining or losing traffic from ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other AI services
・pages with low click-through rates
・articles losing rankings
・high-traffic pages that don’t generate signups
・pages with speed issues
・traffic sources generating signups or purchases

we use NoimosAI agents to continuously identify keyword gaps and rewrite underperforming content.

feed these prompts into NoimosAI to find the gap between you and your competitors:
“Every week, identify high-priority keywords that competitors rank for but we don’t, then create one new article idea.”

“Every month, compare the latest 28 days with the previous 28 days. Use search rankings, clicks, and traffic from AI services to identify the article with the highest improvement potential and create a rewrite plan.”

website optimization isn’t about launching a flashy redesign.

it’s about:

・building a system that measures results
・making your value easy to understand
・creating content around real customer problems
・improving continuously based on data

repeat this process, and your website stops being a static company brochure.

it becomes a system that consistently generates customers.

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network

3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Just in: Tata Sons chairman will not seek re-election, putting major investments in doubt.

N. Chandrasekaran, chairman of Tata Sons, the holding company of Tata Group, will not seek re-election. The leadership change puts the conglomerate’s major investments in semiconductors, Apple iPhone assembly and Air India under renewed scrutiny.

During Chandrasekaran’s tenure, Tata Group made several of what he recently called its “largest capital investments ever.” He described the projects as foundational to India’s effort to become a developed country by 2047. But all of the group’s major new ventures remain in the early stages of investment and have yet to become profitable.

Tata Group acquired loss-making state-owned airline Air India in 2022. After acquiring production capacity associated with Wistron and Pegatron, Tata also began assembling iPhones. Reports have said its scale has surpassed Foxconn’s Indian operations, making Tata India’s largest Apple contract manufacturer.

In 2024, Tata announced a partnership with Taiwan’s Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp. to invest $11 billion in India’s first wafer-fabrication plant. The plan is part of India’s ambition to become a core supply base and eventually challenge China’s role in global manufacturing.

Chandrasekaran’s departure has increased uncertainty around both the semiconductor project and that broader objective. The conglomerate spans software and steel and owns luxury-car maker Jaguar Land Rover. Its core cash-generating business, Tata Consultancy Services, is facing pressure as artificial intelligence disrupts the information-technology industry.

Critics say management is continuing to make aggressive bets on new projects despite the possibility of further losses. Ruchir Hari, chief investment officer of investment-management firm Two X Capital, said the central dispute between Tata Trusts and Tata Sons concerns continued funding for loss-making businesses.

With the chairman preparing to leave, the market is questioning whether the group can maintain its large, long-term investment program. Hari said Chandrasekaran was the “professional successor” personally chosen by the late Ratan Tata. His departure means the two centers of power may have major differences over Tata Sons’ future direction.

Tata Sons formally began the search for a new chairman on Thursday, the day after Chandrasekaran announced that he would not seek another term. He had been dissatisfied that an extension of his five-year term had remained unresolved.

The Dorabji Tata Trust, part of the core trusts that collectively hold 66% of Tata Sons, said it respected Chandrasekaran’s decision not to stand for re-election and would fully support a “smooth, timely and orderly leadership transition.” In a resignation letter submitted Wednesday, Chandrasekaran said a proposal to extend his term had been stalled for six

months and ultimately failed “because one director did not support it.” Local media reported that he had clashed with Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts, over the group’s weakening profitability and the continued flow of capital into loss-making businesses.

According to Tata Sons’ latest annual report, consolidated net profit fell 35% to 266 billion rupees, or about $2.78 billion, in the fiscal year ended March 2026. The decline was dragged down by continuing losses at Air India, Tata Digital and Tata Electronics. All three loss-making businesses are unlisted.

Over the same period, the combined market value of Tata Group’s listed companies fell 12% as investors became more concerned about the group’s long-term growth prospects. Shares of leading IT company TCS also pulled back. Tata Sons did not respond to a request for comment, and Tata Trusts did not respond to questions about the capital-allocation dispute.

Anil Sood, a professor and co-founder of the Mumbai Institute of Complex Choices, said the group’s main profit engine, its IT business, is facing disruption from AI. Tata Trusts, which relies on Tata Sons for returns, wants the group’s capital-allocation strategy to become more conservative, he said. Sood cited the Air India acquisition as an example.

The airline continues to consume substantial amounts of cash, while repeated operational problems are “damaging the Tata brand’s reputation,” he said. At the same time, the group is continuing to expand in manufacturing businesses that are becoming increasingly similar, even as its high-cash-flow, high-margin IT-services business faces disruption from AI.

Experts said Tata Trusts has the upper hand in the power struggle because it controls the highest-level appointment and removal authority at Tata Sons and has the final say. The dual-power structure produced another leadership crisis a decade ago.

Former chairman Cyrus Mistry was forced out in 2016 after a public confrontation with Ratan Tata, who was then in charge of Tata Trusts. Ramesh Vaidyanathan, managing director at India’s BTG Advaya law firm, said the current situation was deeply ironic.

Mistry had argued for maximizing return on net assets and cutting investment rationally, while Ratan Tata had pushed the company to expand aggressively and launch major new projects, Vaidyanathan said. The positions of the two sides in the boardroom confrontation have now been completely reversed.

The Tata Group has long been shaped by a power struggle between its two main centers of authority. Experts say the current conflict is especially important because the group is midway through a major capital-investment cycle.

The successor to Chandrasekaran will face a difficult task: implementing the strategic shift sought by Tata Trusts while also signaling to capital markets that the group can meet the challenges of a new round of global competition. Tata Sons is scheduled to hold its annual general meeting on Aug.

18, when the board is expected to discuss potential successors. Chandrasekaran’s current term expires in February 2027.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

An engineer has built an app using OpenAI’s Codex to detect potholes in Bengaluru and identify contractors linked to relevant road contracts. 

Government data show that 2,385 people died in pothole-related road accidents across India in 2024.

The engineer installed a dashcam setup to capture video, GPS and accelerometer data while driving. Using Codex, he built an app that logs the readings and sends them to OpenAI, using vision models to detect small, medium and large potholes, including those resembling speed breakers from a distance.

The app scans about 2,900 government contracts to identify contractors associated with specific road stretches. 

According to the engineer, roads under warranty may require repairs without additional government cost.

He said the app generates reports in about four seconds, including photos, geolocation, tender numbers and responsible officers. During one drive to work, it detected 12 potholes and generated records for civic complaints.

text:
A Finnish parliamentarian has been blocked  from entering the UK to give an address on freedom of speech at a  conference this week, following her criminal conviction for “hate  speech” by Finland’s Supreme Court.

Longstanding Christian politician Päivi  Räsänen, who is a member of the Finnish Parliament’s “Friends of the  United Kingdom” group, was due to give a talk in person this week about  freedom of speech, at a religious freedom conference.

However, in July, Räsänen was informed  that her Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) to the UK had been  cancelled, despite her application initially being approved in June.

Räsänen will be forced to speak at the  event virtually on Wednesday and Friday, unless she is granted entry to  the country. The Finnish MP and ADF are now calling on the UK Home  Secretary Shabana Mahmood to make a last-minute intervention, to allow  Räsänen to attend in person on Friday.

This follows the Finnish grandmother and former Interior Minister’s “hate speech” conviction by  the Finnish Supreme Court in March 2026, for expressing her Christian  beliefs on marriage and human sexuality in a 2004 booklet written for  her church.

Räsänen’s criminal conviction was noted with concern by observers around the world, including the US State Department and the US Religious Liberty Commission, which was established by President Donald Trump.

Lutheran Bishop Juhana Pohjola, who was  criminally convicted alongside Räsänen for publishing her booklet, was  also blocked from entering the UK, after his ETA was denied in June.

After her ETA was cancelled, Räsänen  subsequently applied for a full visa and wrote to the UK Home Secretary  personally to ask that it be granted ahead of the conference this week.

To date, Räsänen has not received an  answer from the Home Secretary, and was informed that she would not be  given a response on her visa application in time to travel for the  event.

Räsänen, Bishop Pohjola and the Luther Foundation Finland, who were all convicted in March over Räsänen’s booklet, have appealed their  cases to the European Court of Human Rights, where they will be  represented by free speech legal advocacy organisation Alliance  Defending Freedom.

Räsänen said: “It is shocking that the  UK has blocked me, a democratically elected politician in an allied  European state, from entering the country.

“I was convicted of ‘hate speech’ in  Finland for peacefully expressing my Christian views. This was an  egregious case of state censorship, noted with concern by observers  around the world, including the US State Department and the US Religious  Liberty Commission.

“Even though this unjust conviction is  currently on appeal to the European Court of Human Rights, the UK has  likely refused me travel authorisation on this basis. In doing so, the  UK is punishing me for exercising my fundamental human rights.

“I call on Home Secretary Shabana  Mahmood to urgently intervene to allow me to enter the UK to speak at  this event. There is still time for this censorship to be reversed.”

Lorcán Price, legal counsel for Alliance  Defending Freedom, representing Räsänen, Bishop Pohjola and the Luther  Foundation Finland at the European Court of Human Rights, said: “In essence Päivi Räsänen has been blocked from entering the UK for peacefully expressing her Christian beliefs.

“This is not an isolated incident. The  UK has in the last year blocked a number of mainstream conservative  individuals, politicians, and now even a member of the Finnish  Parliament and a Lutheran bishop, from entering the country. This trend  is yet another example of the severe and escalating censorship crisis in  Great Britain.

“Furthermore, the British state is  increasingly cracking down on the rights of Christians in the UK:  Christians have been criminalised for silently praying, offering to  speak with people, publicly preaching their faith, and now they have  been blocked from entering the country for expressing their views.

“Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood should  act immediately to allow my client to enter the country, to speak in  person at the religious liberty event in Northern Ireland. Any further  silence on the Home Secretary’s part will reinforce to the British  people and observers around the world that this government has a  deep-seated antipathy to free speech.”

Bishop Pohjola said: “It is an Orwellian reality that I was blocked from entering the UK by the British state.

“For a senior Lutheran cleric to be  criminally sanctioned in one European country and blocked from entering  another, for merely publishing a church booklet which peacefully  expressed views the Finnish state disagreed with, is extremely alarming.

“It shows how far our civilisation has  strayed not only from its Christian roots, but even from respecting the  basic human rights of free speech and religious freedom. The two are  undoubtedly related, as a new secular orthodoxy has taken root across  Western countries, under which dissenters are punished harshly.

“I sincerely hope the UK Home  Secretary acts to allow Paivi to enter the country, and that the  European Court of Human Rights upholds our right to free speech.  Peacefully expressing views on marriage and human sexuality that  Christians have always held is not a crime.”

Background

The former Finnish Interior Minister,  medical doctor and grandmother of 12 was criminally prosecuted for  nearly seven years for sharing her Christian beliefs about marriage and  human sexuality in a 2019 tweet and live radio debate, as well as for  authoring a 2004 church booklet, for which she was charged alongside  Bishop Pohjola and the Luther Foundation Finland.

In 2021, Räsänen was formally charged with  “agitation against a minority group” under a section of the Finnish  criminal code titled “war crimes and crimes against humanity”.

Following unanimous acquittals on all  charges by two lower courts in 2022 and 2023, the state prosecutor  appealed again to the Finnish Supreme Court, regarding the tweet and  church booklet.

The case was heard in October 2025, and in  March 2026, in a narrow 3–2 decision, the Supreme Court upheld the  acquittal for the Bible verse tweet, but convicted Räsänen,  Bishop Pohjola and the Luther Foundation Finland for the 2004 booklet.  The radio show charge was not appealed to the Supreme Court, so that  acquittal stands.

The Supreme Court convicted Räsänen under  a law that was introduced years after the booklet was published, and  did so despite the court’s admission that the booklet “did not contain  incitement to violence or comparable threat-like fomenting of hatred”.

Christian Finnish Parliamentarian Blocked From Entering UK To Discuss Free Speech At Religious Liberty Conference

In an alarming display of censorship, the  Supreme Court fined Räsänen, Bishop Pohjola, and the Luther Foundation  Finland several thousand euros each, and ruled that the condemned  statements within the booklet must be “removed from public access and  destroyed”.

The US State Department commented on  Räsänen’s criminal prosecution, prior to her conviction in March: “In a  democracy, no one should face trial for peacefully sharing their  beliefs. text:
LIES! LIES! LIES! @himantabiswa MISLEADS ASSAM AND CONTEMPTS THE COURT IN HIS INTERPRETATION OF KAZIRANGA JUDGEMENT

The people of Assam are being systematically misled. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma is presenting a carefully constructed narrative that the proposal to shrink the Eco-Sensitive Zone around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve from the default 10 km to a mere 1 km (or 1–3 km) is a routine, court-mandated exercise that will harm neither wildlife nor the ecological integrity of this UNESCO World Heritage Site. This claim is false. It is a deliberate distortion of the law, the record of the Gauhati High Court, and the consistent directions of the Supreme Court of India. The real objective is to create legal space for mining and commercial activity in the fragile southern landscape of Kaziranga—activity that has already been repeatedly restrained by the highest court of the land.

What follows is a step-by-step, legally grounded account of the true position:

1. The Foundation: How Kaziranga Became a Protected Area

Kaziranga’s protection is not a recent administrative convenience. It began in the colonial era and was progressively strengthened by independent India’s wildlife law.

In 1905 the area was proposed as a Reserve Forest. It was notified as a Reserved Forest in 1908 and upgraded to a Game Sanctuary in 1916. In 1950 it became a Wildlife Sanctuary. On 11 February 1974, vide Notification No. FOR/WL/722/68 issued under Section 8(1)(b) of the Assam National Park Act, 1968, the Governor of Assam declared an area of approximately 429.93 sq km a National Park with effect from 1 January 1974. The notification contains a precise boundary description by rivers, bearings and distances.

Subsequent additions under Section 35 of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 expanded the Park. On 3 August 2007, Notification No. FRW-6/2007/23 under Section 38V declared the larger landscape a Tiger Reserve: core area 48,203.85 ha (including the original National Park and several additions) and buffer 54,835.55 ha (including further additions, reserved forests and the Laokhowa and Burhachapori Wildlife Sanctuaries), totalling approximately 1,030 sq km.

These notifications fix the legal boundary of the protected area. Any Eco-Sensitive Zone is measured outward from that boundary. The buffer of the Tiger Reserve is an internal management zone; it is not a substitute for the regulatory Eco-Sensitive Zone under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and Supreme Court directions.

2. The Supreme Court’s ESZ Framework

The Supreme Court has repeatedly addressed Eco-Sensitive Zones in the T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad proceedings (W.P. (C) No. 202 of 1995).

On 3 June 2022 the Court directed that every national park and wildlife sanctuary must have a minimum 1 km ESZ measured from its demarcated boundary. Where a wider zone was already prescribed by law or a wider proposal was awaiting final decision, the wider margin would prevail. Crucially, where no State or Union Territory proposal had been submitted, the 10 km buffer zone indicated in the 2006 Goa Foundation order and the 2011 Guidelines would operate, and the entire set of ESZ restrictions would apply until a final decision was taken. Mining inside national parks and wildlife sanctuaries was prohibited.

On 26 April 2023 the Court modified the mandatory 1 km direction. It held that a uniform 1 km zone was not feasible in every case and that the direction would not apply where a draft or final notification had already been issued by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change or where proposals had been received by the Ministry. The Court retained the absolute prohibition on mining within the protected area and within 1 km of its boundary. The 10 km default direction for areas where no proposal had been submitted remained in force.

In short, the Supreme Court never authorised States to unilaterally shrink an existing protective default. It required a formal, site-specific proposal, central scrutiny, and a final notification. Until that process is completed, the 10 km default continues.

3. The Gauhati High Court Record: What the Court Actually Said

Order dated 12 March 2026 (Justice Manish Choudhury) in Jiten Engjai v. Union of India (WP(C)/6479/2025)
This is the order repeatedly invoked by the Chief Minister. The petition challenged the suspension of a stone quarry in the Parkup Pahar Range on the ground that it fell within the default Eco-Sensitive Zone of Kaziranga.

The Court examined the Supreme Court orders of 3 June 2022 and 26 April 2023 in detail. On a specific query, the Standing Counsel for the Environment and Forest Department of Assam submitted that as on 12 March 2026 there was neither any final notification nor any draft proposal on the Eco-Sensitive Zone of Kaziranga National Park from the State Government that had been submitted to the Central Government. The Court therefore held that the 10 km Eco-Sensitive Zone remained operative. Paragraph 61 of the 26 April 2023 order (the exemption for already-notified or proposed ESZs) was held inapplicable.

The Court also recalled the Supreme Court’s 12 April 2019 order restraining all mining and related activities along the southern boundary of Kaziranga and in the entire catchment of rivers, streams and rivulets originating in the Karbi Anglong hills and flowing into the Park, as well as the prohibition on new construction on private lands forming part of the nine identified animal corridors.

Order dated 11 August 2026 (Justice Devashis Baruah) in the batch of connected petitions

This later order deals with the continued suspension of several stone quarries following directions issued by the Central Empowered Committee. The Court noted the sequence of events, including the CEC’s communication of 30 May 2025, and observed that the powers conferred on the CEC under the 5 September 2023 notification appear limited to monitoring and making recommendations rather than issuing binding directions. The Court sought clarification from the Government of India on the scope of the CEC’s authority and listed the matters for further hearing on 3 September 2026. It did not disturb the factual finding of 12 March 2026 that no ESZ proposal for Kaziranga had been submitted and that the 10 km default therefore continued to operate.

4. What Activities Are Prohibited and Permitted in an Eco-Sensitive Zone

Under the 2011 Guidelines and the Supreme Court’s directions:
Prohibited activities include commercial mining, stone quarrying, and related industrial operations; setting up of new major hydro-electric projects; discharge of untreated effluents; and establishment of polluting industries.

Regulated activities include construction (subject to height and density restrictions), tourism facilities, and certain agricultural or forest-related activities, all requiring prior approval.

Permitted activities are limited to those that do not adversely affect the ecology—essentially traditional habitation and certain eco-development works.

Even if a narrower site-specific ESZ is eventually notified, mining remains absolutely prohibited within 1 km of the protected-area boundary. The Supreme Court has been consistent on this point. Any attempt to portray a reduction of the buffer as authorising mining closer to Kaziranga is legally false.

5. The Pattern of Illegal Mining and the Name of RS Gandhi

The southern landscape of Kaziranga has long been plagued by illegal stone and sand mining. The Supreme Court’s 12 April 2019 order was itself based on reports of such activity. The Central Empowered Committee has repeatedly recorded that mining continued and even intensified despite the ban. In 2025 the CEC reported fresh permissions granted by the Karbi Anglong Autonomous Council in violation of the Supreme Court’s directions and without the required approvals under the Forest (Conservation) Act.

Ranbir Singh Gandhi (RS Gandhi) of Hills Trade Agencies has been named in petitions before the Supreme Court and in public complaints as a prominent operator of stone quarries in Assam, including in areas under scrutiny near the Kaziranga landscape (Jagiroad, Panimara and related sites). Courts and the CEC have taken cognisance of these allegations. The pattern is clear: despite judicial restraints, commercial mining interests continue to press against the southern boundary of the Park. What is his relation to @Pijush_hazarika 

6. Why Protection Is More Urgent Than Ever: Rare Earth Elements

The Geological Survey of India has identified significant Rare Earth Element resources in the Jashora Ultramafic Alkaline Complex and the Samchampi-Samteran belt in Karbi Anglong. It is precisely the landscape that forms the southern refuge for Kaziranga’s wildlife during floods. Resource estimates of the order of 28.64 million tonnes have been reported at G3 level, with further exploration under way. These critical minerals are of strategic national importance. Their presence only heightens the need for rigorous ecological safeguards. 

Any weakening of the buffer around Kaziranga risks opening the door to mining pressures that could permanently damage the hydrology, wildlife corridors and floodplain ecology of one of the world’s most important protected areas.

7. The Political Deception

Himanta Biswa Sarma claims that a 10 km zone would “finish” towns such as Bokakhat, Kaliabor and Jakhalabandha and even force the closure of the Numaligarh Refinery. This is scare-mongering. The 10 km default has operated for years without extinguishing these settlements. The Supreme Court itself recognised in 2023 that day-to-day activities of citizens should not be unduly hampered, while simultaneously insisting that mining near protected areas remains forbidden.

The Chief Minister’s insistence that the State is merely following Supreme Court directions ignores the High Court’s own record: as of March 2026 the State had submitted no proposal at all. The sudden urgency to notify a narrow zone, while stone quarries remain under active judicial scrutiny and while rare-earth exploration intensifies in the same hills, reveals the real priority—facilitating commercial extraction under the cover of a “scientific” notification.

Kaziranga is not merely a tourist destination or a political talking point. It is the last major stronghold of the one-horned rhinoceros, a critical tiger habitat, and an irreplaceable floodplain ecosystem. Animals do not recognise administrative lines drawn on maps; during the annual floods they move into the Karbi Anglong foothills. A 1 km buffer offers them no meaningful refuge once mining, crushers and industrial activity occupy the adjoining landscape.

The @INCAssam  demands that the State Government immediately place before the public and the courts the complete scientific basis, if any, for the proposed 1 km zone; that all mining and related activities in the southern catchment remain strictly restrained in accordance with the Supreme Court’s 2019 and subsequent directions; and that the ecological integrity of Kaziranga not be sacrificed for short-term commercial gain. The people of Assam deserve the truth, not carefully packaged misrepresentation.

text:
Adani and India’s Forests: A Decade of Protests, Tree Felling and Tribal Resistance

For nearly a decade, the Adani Group has faced sustained opposition from tribal communities, environmental activists and civil-society organisations over coal-mining projects affecting forest areas in India. The most prominent and persistent struggle has taken place in the Hasdeo Arand forests of Chhattisgarh, where protests have continued through successive state governments.

The Hasdeo conflict is not a recent development. The roots go back to the early 2010s, when forest clearance was sought for the Parsa East and Kente Basan (PEKB) coal blocks. The blocks were allotted to Rajasthan's power utility, while Adani Enterprises became the mine developer and operator. Forest clearance for the first phase was granted in 2012.

As mining expanded, local Adivasi communities increasingly organised against further forest diversion. They argued that the forests were essential for farming, collection of forest produce, cultural practices and wildlife, and that further mining would fragment elephant habitat.

The movement became particularly visible in 2021. Villagers from the Hasdeo region travelled to Delhi to protest the proposed diversion of about 841.5 hectares of forest for the Parsa coal mine. The protesters demanded protection of their forests and questioned the validity of Gram Sabha consent.

In October 2021, Adivasi residents organised a roughly 300-kilometre march from the Hasdeo forests to Chhattisgarh's capital, Raipur. The movement brought the forest dispute into national political attention and attracted support from environmental organisations and political groups.

The protests intensified in 2022 when authorities moved forward with expansion of the existing PEKB mine. The Chhattisgarh Assembly passed a resolution supporting cancellation of coal blocks in Hasdeo, while the then state government also wrote to the Centre seeking cancellation of forest clearance for the Parsa block, citing widespread public protests and a law-and-order situation.

Despite these political developments, mining and tree-felling remained a continuing source of conflict. Indian Express reported that nearly 96,000 trees had officially been cut for PEKB since 2012, while activists claimed the actual number was considerably higher.

The situation again became highly contentious after the 2023 Chhattisgarh election. Tree-felling resumed in areas proposed for further expansion, leading to renewed demonstrations by local residents and environmental groups.

In October 2024, the confrontation reached another critical point when villagers opposing tree-felling for the Parsa coal project clashed with police. Reports said 13 police personnel and several villagers were injured. The proposed Parsa block contains substantial forest land and is operated by an Adani Group company as mine developer and operator for the Rajasthan government-owned power utility.

The protests have centred heavily on the Forest Rights Act and the role of Gram Sabhas. Villagers have repeatedly argued that their consent is legally required before forest resources and traditional lands are diverted for commercial mining. Some residents and activists have alleged that consent documents were improperly obtained or forged—claims that have been disputed and remain part of the broader legal and political controversy.

Hasdeo is not the only environmental controversy involving the Adani Group. In Uttar Pradesh, an Adani power project in Mirzapur has faced proceedings before the National Green Tribunal after an environmental activist alleged that construction was taking place on forest land and could damage the local environment. Adani has denied the allegations and maintained that the project land is not forest land.

Adani's projects have also generated environmental opposition outside India. The Carmichael coal mine in Queensland, Australia, became the focus of a major seven-year "Stop Adani" campaign involving environmental organisations and local communities. The campaign ran from roughly 2015 to 2022 and became one of Australia's most prominent anti-coal movements.

Back in India, the Hasdeo movement has increasingly become a symbol of the larger debate over "jal, jungle, zameen"—water, forests and land. Supporters of the protests argue that economic development and energy security cannot justify the destruction of ecologically important forests or the displacement of indigenous communities.

The government and project supporters, on the other hand, point to India's enormous demand for electricity, industrial development and coal. Adani has also disputed allegations of environmental wrongdoing in individual cases, making clear that several of the controversies remain contested rather than legally settled.

The controversy entered another phase in 2025–26. Forest diversion for additional coal mining in the Hasdeo region again attracted opposition from environmental activists and political groups. Reports in 2026 described large tribal and farmers' demonstrations in Chhattisgarh against mining projects and alleged violations of forest and land rights.

The dispute has therefore lasted far longer than a single mining project or a single government. For local communities, the decade-long movement is fundamentally about whether forests can survive industrial expansion and whether Adivasi communities will have a decisive voice over land they have traditionally depended upon.

For Adani, the Hasdeo controversy represents one of the most persistent environmental and community conflicts surrounding its Indian coal business. For India's environmental movement, it has become a defining case in the continuing struggle between coal-driven development, forest conservation and tribal rights.

The story is still unfolding. With new mining clearances, continuing court proceedings, tree-felling disputes and renewed protests, Hasdeo remains one of India's most closely watched battles over forests, coal and the future of indigenous communities.

I have filed a complaint with the Grievance Officer of YouTube against those bloggers as per the IT Rules, as directed by the Delhi High Court. The time limit for the Grievance Officer to act on the complaint is 15 days from the date of receipt. If YouTube does not take action, there is a Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) where we can challenge the decision of the Grievance Officer. text:
UPDATE TO ALL MEMBERS ON LOCUM ENGAGEMENT & CASUALIZATION

The leadership of NARD, ably led by the Strategic P-MUS (Garkuwan Matasan Arewa), is pleased to update members on the outcome of the FMoHSW Committee on  Regulation and Casualization of Doctors.

Following extensive consultations, the Committee has developed a National Policy on the Engagement of Locum, aimed at ensuring fair, transparent and non-exploitative engagement of temporary healthcare personnel.

KEY RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Recruitment & Approval:
   Locum engagement must be based on a clearly identified staffing gap and approved by the appropriate hospital authorities.

2. Contract Duration:
   Initial locum contracts shall not exceed 6 months, with only one additional 6-month renewal permitted. Continuous engagement for 12 months makes the position eligible for permanent appointment.

3. Maximum Work Hours:
   Healthcare personnel shall work a maximum of 48 hours per week, including weekends. Excess hours must be appropriately compensated.

4. Maximum Duty Period:
   No healthcare personnel shall work beyond 24 continuous hours, including call duty.

5. Mandatory Rest:
   
   - Minimum 12 hours between shifts.

   - Mandatory 24-hour post-call rest after weekday and weekend calls.

   - A 1-hour break after 6 hours of continuous work.

6. Call Duty:
   
   - Maximum 2 calls per week.

   - Maximum 1 weekend call per month.

   - Calls must be equitably distributed.

7. Remuneration & Welfare:
Pay rates are standardized in alignment with the government's 
Scheme of Service. Remuneration must be paid monthly without delay, accompanied by monthly 
payslips. 

Locum staff are entitled to all government-approved leaves, public holidays, and occupational insurance coverage.

8. Excess Work Hours:
   Excess hours must be properly documented, monitored and adequately compensated, or appropriately balanced with structured time-off.

9. Protection Against Abuse:
   Locum engagement must not be used as a permanent substitute for substantive recruitment or as a means of exploiting healthcare workers.

10. Integration & Safety: All locum workers must undergo mandatory orientation and integration into their respective clinical or administrative teams. Institutions are required to provide safe 
working environment, adequate call rooms, refreshments during prolonged calls/shifts, and burnout prevention programs.

11. Discipline & Grievance Process: Professional misconduct shall be governed by the regulatory 
council guidelines. Contracts can be terminated by either party with a one-month notice or payment in lieu, and all accrued entitlements must be settled within 14 days of termination. Disputes escalate through institutional mechanisms up to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, and the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment.

12. Monitoring: The Ministry would ensure Institutions do not engage in exploitative staffing practices and violations of this guideline in line with the Nigerian Labour Law.

13. Policy Review and Effective Date:
This policy becomes legally binding on the exact date of approval by the Federal Ministry of 
Health and Social Welfare (FMoH&SW). To ensure its continuous operational relevance, the 
policy mandates a comprehensive evaluation and review within two (2) years of its 
implementation.

The policy is expected to provide a more structured and equitable framework for locum engagement across Nigerian health institutions.

Appreciation to the Hon. Coordinating Minister for Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Mohammad Ali Pate for this approval.

Special appreciation to the Hon. Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Dr. Iziak Adekunle Salako for his guidance and dictation to seeing this through.

Appreciations are also in order to our distinguished NARDites in the Committee for a job well done. Thank you Dr. Kwarshak Kevin Yakubu, the VP 2 of NARD. Thank you Dr. Shuaibu Ibrahim, the Secretary General of NARD.

NARD is particularly proud of this accomplishments and proves once again what we can achieve when we come together as a team.

NARD remains committed to protecting the dignity, welfare, rights and professional interests of every Nigerian doctor.

It is our hope that the National Council on Health will also give their stamp of approval on this.

Dr. Abdulmajid Yahya Ibrahim
NARD PSS

An insurer’s obligation under Section 10 is statutory not merely contractual.**

In  Ringera v Directline Assurance Co. Ltd, Civil Case No. E155 of 2026, the Court held that once judgment is entered against an insured person in respect of a liability falling within Section 5(b) of the Insurance (Motor Vehicle Third Party Risks) Act, and the statutory conditions under Section 10 are satisfied, the insurer is under a statutory obligation to satisfy the judgment.

That obligation extends to the judgment sum, costs and applicable interest.

The decree does not become enforceable against the insurer merely because judgment exists. The statutory gateway under Section 10 must first be satisfied.
